topic: cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning; value decomposition; relative overgeneralization
status: bounded comparison of two sampled papers and one targeted AAAI-26 primary-source follow-up
claim: Three distinct approaches relax or remove monotonic value-factorization constraints, but their results do not establish a universal benefit: NQMIX uses an actor/off-policy policy-gradient hybrid and reports three-run results on three selected SMAC maps; GVR uses inferior-target shaping and superior replay, reports five-seed benchmarks, and derives an exploration threshold that becomes impractical as agents/actions grow; a 2026 AAAI paper analyzes a separate unconstrained Q-learning method under approximately-greedy exploration. The testable research opportunity is a matched mechanism-by-exploration-by-scale comparison, not simply another unconstrained mixer.
positive_evidence: NQMIX beats QMIX and COMA on the two complex heterogeneous-unit SMAC maps shown, with an ablation indicating that the mixer modification affects results.
GVR reports matrix-game, predator-prey and SMAC results; its formal analysis specifies conditions for eliminating non-optimal self-transition nodes.

The AAAI-26 primary-source paper gives a separate continuous-time stability analysis and reports experiments on matrix games, SMAC and Google Research Football, with five independent runs for benchmark win-rate curves.
counterevidence: NQMIX's main comparisons use only three independent runs and selected maps; the authors request broader maps and flag an actor bottleneck.

GVR states the sufficient exploration threshold approaches 1 as team size/action count increase and says this can be inapplicable to long-episode tasks; its optional trade-off hurts some difficult tasks.
The AAAI-26 formal analysis is a single-state game with a unique global optimum and smooth/regularity assumptions, not an unconditional convergence theorem for arbitrary deep partially observed MARL.

sources.sections: Sections 5–6, Appendix B: SMAC results, three-run count, ablation and future work
Sections 3–5, Appendix H and J: GVR conditions, exploration scaling, benchmark results and limitations

sources.title: Beyond Monotonicity: Revisiting Factorization Principles in Multi-Agent Q-Learning

falsifiable_test: Implement NQMIX, GVR, the 2026 unconstrained SARSA-style method, QMIX and a strong expressive baseline with matched parameters, environment steps, compute, exploration schedule and seeds. Sweep agent count, local action count, episode horizon, reward sparsity, and task class; report team return, globally optimal joint-action rate, win rate, sample/compute efficiency, variance, and divergence. The broad advantage claim weakens if it disappears at matched budget or larger held-out scales; it strengthens if each mechanism has a repeatable regime of advantage with measurable predictors. No implementation or experiment was run in this literature audit.
limitations: Two sampled papers plus one later primary-source paper; distinct algorithms and benchmark setups are not a head-to-head comparison. The AAAI theory is conditional and single-state; conclusions should not be generalized to all cooperative MARL.

topic: multi-agent reinforcement learning; exploration; scalable coordination
status: bounded evidence synthesis from one sampled ICML full text
claim: GVR's unique-optimal-self-transition result relies on sufficient conditions involving exploration. Its appendix derives a threshold that approaches 1 as the number of agents and individual action choices increase, says the required large exploration can be inapplicable to long-episode tasks, and reports optional stability/optimality trade-off settings that can underperform on difficult tasks. This makes exploration cost and critic conflict concrete scale limits to test, not evidence that GVR fails generally.
positive_evidence: The paper provides a theoretical threshold for a sufficient exploration condition and empirical matrix-game/predator-prey/SMAC results.
GVR reports favorable outcomes against several baselines on its tested tasks and uses five seeds for its main SMAC comparisons.
counterevidence: The threshold is sufficient, not necessarily necessary; its high value alone does not prove all practical exploration schedules fail.
GVR succeeds on its tested benchmarks, and its poor trade-off results are confined to some hard tasks/settings.

sources.sections: Section 4 and Appendix H/J: exploration threshold, multiple-superior-action cases, trade-off, seed/setup details

falsifiable_test: Scale agent count, per-agent action count, horizon and exploration schedule in matrix, predator-prey and SMAC-like tasks. Measure whether the predicted sufficient epsilon threshold tracks empirical unique-optimal convergence, training steps, return variance and instability; ablate ITS, SER and the trade-off critics. The practical concern weakens if stable low-cost schedules attain the same guarantee as scale grows; it strengthens if the threshold predicts exploding sample cost or loss of stability. No algorithm was reimplemented here.
limitations: One sampled paper; threshold is sufficient and derived for particular assumptions, and observed failure may depend on task, implementation and schedule.

topic: multi-agent state estimation; distributed set-membership filtering; research provenance
status: withdrawal-source audit plus one distinct same-author conference-paper full-text follow-up
claim: The sampled arXiv record 2305.15797 is withdrawn; arXiv provides no PDF for its withdrawn version, and the authors state that equations 4–6 were not fully correctly derived and underpin the marginal-based framework. Its abstract-level claims are therefore not counted as verified evidence. A distinct 2023 same-author paper, 2305.10366, provides related constrained-zonotope centralized/distributed state-estimation methods and a five-UAV simulation, but has more conservative sets than the centralized baseline and is not a correction or validation of the withdrawn derivation.
positive_evidence: The official arXiv record states that v2 is withdrawn, no PDF is available, and the authors identify the derivation of equations 4–6 as not fully correct.
The separate 2305.10366 paper proves/sets out centralized and distributed algorithms and illustrates containment of simulated UAV positions using local absolute/relative measurements.
counterevidence: The arXiv page is primary evidence of withdrawal but not an independent mathematical proof that the derivation is wrong.
The same-author related 2023 paper is a separate method and does not by itself establish the cause, scope or correction of the 2305.15797 error.
The available distributed-estimation evidence is a five-agent simulation; it is not a physical UAV field validation.

sources.sections: Official arXiv submission history, PDF availability and author withdrawal comment
Sections III–VI: algorithms, five-UAV simulation, set-size comparison and future work

falsifiable_test: Trace citations and publication records for 2305.15797, locate any corrected manuscript or erratum, and compare its disputed equations line-by-line with 2305.10366 and subsequent journal work. The concern weakens if an independently checked corrected version resolves the derivation and reproduces results; it strengthens if downstream papers rely on the withdrawn equations or no correction exists. No independent derivation audit was conducted here.
limitations: This is a provenance and literature-integrity finding, not a mathematical adjudication. The withdrawn sample lacks a locally available PDF; follow-up evidence is related, not a replication.
